claim: The bone-resorbing activity of osteoclasts plays a critical role in the life-long remodeling of our bones that is perturbed in many bone loss diseases.
source: The bone-resorbing activity of osteoclasts plays a critical role in the life-long remodeling of our bones that is perturbed in many bone loss diseases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about osteoclast function in bone remodeling and disease.

claim: Multinucleated osteoclasts are formed by the fusion of precursor cells.
source: Multinucleated osteoclasts are formed by the fusion of precursor cells
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about osteoclast formation.

claim: Larger osteoclasts generated by an increased number of cell fusion events have higher resorptive activity.
source: larger cells – generated by an increased number of cell fusion events – have higher resorptive activity
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Piper et al., 1992; Møller et al., 2020).

claim: Osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are promoted by reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling.
source: We find that osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are promoted by reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are promoted by an unconventional low molecular weight species of La protein located at the osteoclast surface.
source: We find that osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are promoted by reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and by an unconventional low molecular weight species of La protein, located at the osteoclast surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and builds on previous work (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Differentiating osteoclasts enrich an oxidized species of La at the cell surface.
source: we find that differentiating osteoclasts enrich an oxidized species of La at the cell surface
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data using redox-specific antibodies shown in Figure 1.

claim: The oxidized La species at the cell surface is distinct from the reduced La species conventionally localized within cell nuclei.
source: we find that differentiating osteoclasts enrich an oxidized species of La at the cell surface, which is distinct from the reduced La species conventionally localized within cell nuclei
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data using redox-specific antibodies shown in Figure 1.

claim: ROS signaling triggers the shift from reduced to oxidized La species.
source: ROS signaling triggers the shift from reduced to oxidized La species
evidence: This is supported by NAC treatment experiments shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROS signaling triggers La dephosphorylation.
source: ROS signaling triggers the shift from reduced to oxidized La species, its dephosphorylation
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a,b showing increased phosphorylated La with NAC treatment.

claim: ROS signaling triggers delivery of La to the surface of osteoclasts.
source: ROS signaling triggers the shift from reduced to oxidized La species, its dephosphorylation and delivery to the surface of osteoclasts
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5e showing reduced surface La with NAC treatment.

claim: Surface La promotes multinucleation of osteoclasts.
source: delivery to the surface of osteoclasts, where La promotes multinucleation
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 showing antibody inhibition of fusion and previous work (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Surface La promotes resorptive activity of osteoclasts.
source: delivery to the surface of osteoclasts, where La promotes multinucleation and resorptive activity
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3c showing resorption assays and previous work (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Intracellular ROS signaling in differentiating osteoclasts oxidizes critical cysteine residues in the C-terminal half of La.
source: intracellular ROS signaling in differentiating osteoclasts oxidizes critical cysteine residues in the C-terminal half of La
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing loss of function with cysteine mutations and Figure 6 showing rescue experiments.

claim: Oxidation of critical cysteine residues in the C-terminal half of La produces an unconventional La species that promotes osteoclast fusion.
source: intracellular ROS signaling in differentiating osteoclasts oxidizes critical cysteine residues in the C-terminal half of La, producing this unconventional La species that promotes osteoclast fusion
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing loss of fusion promotion with cysteine mutations.

claim: The integrity of bones throughout life depends on tightly regulated coordination between the bone-forming activity of osteoblasts and the bone-resorbing activity of osteoclasts.
source: The integrity of our bones throughout life depends on tightly regulated coordination between the bone-forming activity of osteoblasts and the bone-resorbing activity of osteoclasts (Kim et al., 2020; McDonald et al., 2021; Bolamperti et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A variety of genetic and age-related skeletal disorders are linked to a disbalance in osteoblast–osteoclast functional coupling.
source: A variety of genetic and age-related skeletal disorders are linked to a disbalance in osteoblast–osteoclast functional coupling that commonly results in excessive bone resorption and/or insufficient synthesis and mineralization of bone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about skeletal disorders.

claim: In most cases, osteoclasts with more nuclei have higher resorptive activity.
source: in most cases, cells with more nuclei (i.e., generated by a larger number of fusion events) have higher resorptive activity (Piper et al., 1992; Møller et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are controlled by an unconventional, low molecular weight form of La protein.
source: We recently demonstrated that both osteoclast fusion and bone resorption are controlled by an unconventional, low molecular weight form of La protein (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: La exists primarily as a phosphorylated, nuclear species that plays essential functions in the maturation of RNA polymerase III transcripts, particularly tRNA.
source: La (SSB small RNA-binding exonuclease protection factor La, Gene ID 6741, NCBI GENE), an abundant, ubiquitous protein in eukaryotes, exists primarily as a phosphorylated, nuclear species that plays essential functions in the maturation of RNA polymerase III transcripts, particularly tRNA (Wolin and Cedervall, 2002; Maraia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about La protein supported by citations.

claim: La is dephosphorylated, proteolytically cleaved, and delivered to the surface of osteoclasts during multinucleation.
source: However, we discovered that La is dephosphorylated, proteolytically cleaved, and delivered to the surface of osteoclasts during multinucleation.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Surface-associated La promotes cell–cell fusion in osteoclasts.
source: Surface-associated La promotes cell–cell fusion and increased resorptive capacity in osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Surface-associated La promotes increased resorptive capacity in osteoclasts.
source: Surface-associated La promotes cell–cell fusion and increased resorptive capacity in osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: When osteoclasts reach a mature size appropriate for their biological activity, fusion stops.
source: When osteoclasts reach a mature size appropriate for their biological activity, fusion stops.
evidence: This is an observation from previous work by the authors (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Completion of the fusion process coincides with the removal of surface-associated La.
source: Completion of the fusion process coincides with the removal of surface-associated La
evidence: This is an observation from previous work by the authors (Whitlock et al., 2023).

claim: Changes in the surface La amounts effectively set the size and biological activity of osteoclasts.
source: Completion of the fusion process coincides with the removal of surface-associated La, suggesting that the changes in the surface La amounts effectively set the size and biological activity of osteoclasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of La removal coinciding with fusion completion.

claim: Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) represents a common biological switch for proteins with multiple functions in eukaryotes.
source: Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) represents a common biological switch for proteins with multiple functions in eukaryotes (Dishman and Volkman, 2018; Liu and Jeffery, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Excessive levels of ROS during oxidative stress eventually lead to irreversible damage of biological systems and tissues.
source: Excessive levels of ROS during oxidative stress eventually lead to irreversible damage of biological systems and tissues and have been linked to diverse diseases in many physiological systems, including the skeleton (Forman and Zhang, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Excessive levels of ROS have been linked to diverse diseases in many physiological systems, including the skeleton.
source: Excessive levels of ROS during oxidative stress eventually lead to irreversible damage of biological systems and tissues and have been linked to diverse diseases in many physiological systems, including the skeleton (Forman and Zhang, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Transient, moderate increases in ROS levels play important roles in diverse cellular differentiation processes.
source: However, transient, moderate increases in ROS levels, referred to as redox signaling (Schieber and Chandel, 2014; Lennicke and Cochemé, 2021) or a mild oxidative stress (Ďuračková, 2010), play important roles in diverse cellular differentiation processes (Forman et al., 2010; Wilson, 2014; Domazetovic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intracellular ROS signaling commonly induces the formation of disulfide bonds.
source: Intracellular ROS signaling commonly induces the formation of disulfide bonds, drives structural and oligomeric transitions, and promotes the unconventional secretion of some proteins lacking a signal peptide (Urano et al., 2018; Kwak et al., 2019; Cruz-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Intracellular ROS signaling drives structural and oligomeric transitions in proteins.
source: Intracellular ROS signaling commonly induces the formation of disulfide bonds, drives structural and oligomeric transitions, and promotes the unconventional secretion of some proteins lacking a signal peptide (Urano et al., 2018; Kwak et al., 2019; Cruz-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Intracellular ROS signaling promotes the unconventional secretion of some proteins lacking a signal peptide.
source: Intracellular ROS signaling commonly induces the formation of disulfide bonds, drives structural and oligomeric transitions, and promotes the unconventional secretion of some proteins lacking a signal peptide (Urano et al., 2018; Kwak et al., 2019; Cruz-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A transition in the redox state of cysteine residues can be triggered by protein trafficking changes that shift the localization of a protein from the cytosol to the extracellular environment.
source: Alternatively, a transition in the redox state of cysteine residues can also be triggered merely by protein trafficking changes that shifts the localization of a protein from the cytosol (typically reducing) to the extracellular environment (typically oxidizing) (Gilbert, 1990; Ottaviano et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Bone remodeling depends on ROS signaling.
source: Like many other physiological processes, bone remodeling and, more specifically, osteoclast formation depend on ROS signaling (Domazetovic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Osteoclast formation depends on ROS signaling.
source: Like many other physiological processes, bone remodeling and, more specifically, osteoclast formation depend on ROS signaling (Domazetovic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RANKL-induced differentiation of osteoclast precursors quickly generates transient ROS signaling in differentiating osteoclasts.
source: Receptor activator of NF-kappaB ligand (RANKL)-induced differentiation of osteoclast precursors quickly generates transient ROS signaling in differentiating osteoclasts (Lee et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Many bone diseases, including osteoporosis, have been linked to perturbations in ROS signaling.
source: many bone diseases, including osteoporosis, have been linked to perturbations in ROS signaling (Domazetovic et al., 2017; Reis and Ramos, 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Application of oxidizing reagents, such as H2O2, promotes osteoclast formation.
source: Moreover, application of oxidizing reagents, such as H2O2, promotes osteoclast formation (Suda et al., 1993; Agidigbi and Kim, 2019; Bartell et al., 2014; Lean et al., 2005; Garrett et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cell-permeable antioxidants block RANKL-induced ROS production.
source: In contrast, cell-permeable antioxidants block RANKL-induced ROS production and inhibit osteoclast formation and bone resorption (Huh et al., 2006; Sanders et al., 2007; Cao and Picklo, 2014; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cell-permeable antioxidants inhibit osteoclast formation.
source: In contrast, cell-permeable antioxidants block RANKL-induced ROS production and inhibit osteoclast formation and bone resorption (Huh et al., 2006; Sanders et al., 2007; Cao and Picklo, 2014; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cell-permeable antioxidants inhibit bone resorption.
source: In contrast, cell-permeable antioxidants block RANKL-induced ROS production and inhibit osteoclast formation and bone resorption (Huh et al., 2006; Sanders et al., 2007; Cao and Picklo, 2014; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Oxidizing conditions and intracellular redox signaling elicit conformational transitions and oligomerization of La protein.
source: Recent biochemical studies demonstrate that oxidizing conditions and intracellular redox signaling elicit conformational transitions and oligomerization of La protein and promote its nucleus-to-cytoplasm shuttling (Berndt et al., 2021a; Berndt et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Oxidizing conditions and intracellular redox signaling promote La protein's nucleus-to-cytoplasm shuttling.
source: Recent biochemical studies demonstrate that oxidizing conditions and intracellular redox signaling elicit conformational transitions and oligomerization of La protein and promote its nucleus-to-cytoplasm shuttling (Berndt et al., 2021a; Berndt et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear La and cell surface La in differentiating osteoclasts represent reduced and oxidized species of the protein, respectively.
source: Using antibodies that recognize reduced vs oxidized species of La, we found that nuclear La and cell surface La in differentiating osteoclasts to represent reduced and oxidized species of the protein, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Oxidized La species at the surface of osteoclasts promoted their fusion and increased multinucleation.
source: Oxidized La species at the surface of osteoclasts promoted their fusion and increased multinucleation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors inhibited the appearance of La in the cytoplasm.
source: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors inhibited the appearance of La in the cytoplasm and at the surface of osteoclasts and suppressed fusion during osteoclast formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors inhibited the appearance of La at the surface of osteoclasts.
source: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors inhibited the appearance of La in the cytoplasm and at the surface of osteoclasts and suppressed fusion during osteoclast formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 5e.

claim: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors suppressed fusion during osteoclast formation.
source: Suppressing ROS signaling in osteoclast precursors inhibited the appearance of La in the cytoplasm and at the surface of osteoclasts and suppressed fusion during osteoclast formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 5d.

claim: Addition of the C-terminal half of La to the extracellular surface of osteoclasts rescued ROS suppression-mediated inhibition of fusion, but only if critical La cysteine residues were available for oxidation.
source: Addition of the C-terminal half of La – the region required for promoting osteoclast fusion (Whitlock et al., 2023) – to the extracellular surface of osteoclasts rescued this inhibition but only if critical La cysteine residues were available for oxidation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: At the time of fusion, La is present in both the cytoplasm and nuclei of permeabilized osteoclasts.
source: At the time of fusion, immunofluorescence analysis of La's localization in permeabilized osteoclasts with pan α-La antibody demonstrated that La is present in both the cytoplasm and nuclei (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The cytoplasmic/plasma membrane-associated pool of La is recognized by the α-La antibody that recognizes oxidized La species.
source: In stark contrast, the cytoplasmic/plasma membrane-associated pool was recognized by the α-La antibody that recognizes oxidized La species, while the α-La antibody that recognizes reduced La species recognized the nuclear protein pool (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nuclear pool of La is recognized by the α-La antibody that recognizes reduced La species.
source: In stark contrast, the cytoplasmic/plasma membrane-associated pool was recognized by the α-La antibody that recognizes oxidized La species, while the α-La antibody that recognizes reduced La species recognized the nuclear protein pool (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: La is readily observed at the surface of fusing osteoclasts under non-permeabilizing conditions.
source: Under non-permeabilizing conditions – focusing on the exofacial surface of the plasma membrane – we readily observed La at the surface of fusing osteoclasts (see also Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b and previous work.

claim: The surface pool of La is dramatically enriched in oxidized, rather than reduced, La species.
source: We find that this surface pool of La is dramatically enriched in oxidized, rather than reduced, La species (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Application of the membrane-impermeable reducing reagent TCEP dramatically decreased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized species.
source: In further support of this conclusion, we found that application of the membrane-impermeable reducing reagent Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP) dramatically decreased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized species and increased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the reduced species (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Application of the membrane-impermeable reducing reagent TCEP increased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the reduced species.
source: In further support of this conclusion, we found that application of the membrane-impermeable reducing reagent Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP) dramatically decreased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized species and increased the recognition of surface La by the α-La antibody that recognizes the reduced species (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: TCEP had no effect on the ability of the pan α-La antibody to recognize surface La.
source: In contrast, TCEP had no effect on the ability of the pan α-La antibody to recognize surface La (Figure 1b, c)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: TCEP treatment did not dissociate cell surface La from plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, TCEP treatment did not dissociate cell surface La from plasma membrane, suggesting that the reduced species of La retains its ability to associate with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from the data in Figure 1.

claim: The reduced species of La retains its ability to associate with the plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, TCEP treatment did not dissociate cell surface La from plasma membrane, suggesting that the reduced species of La retains its ability to associate with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TCEP does not dissociate La from the membrane.

claim: Pan α-La antibody 5B9 applied at the time of LPC removal inhibited synchronized osteoclast fusion.
source: As we demonstrated previously with another pan α-La antibody (Whitlock et al., 2023), pan α-La antibody 5B9 applied at the time of LPC removal inhibited synchronized osteoclast fusion (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b and previous work.

claim: α-La antibodies that recognize the oxidized species inhibited synchronized osteoclast fusion.
source: Similarly, α-La antibodies that recognize the oxidized species inhibited fusion, while antibodies that recognize the reduced La species had no effect on fusion (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Antibodies that recognize the reduced La species had no effect on synchronized osteoclast fusion.
source: Similarly, α-La antibodies that recognize the oxidized species inhibited fusion, while antibodies that recognize the reduced La species had no effect on fusion (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Reducing the surface of human osteoclasts via TCEP treatment inhibits synchronized osteoclast fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In further support of the functional importance of surface La oxidation, and possibly other surface proteins, we find that reducing the surface of human osteoclasts via TCEP treatment – which reduces surface La but does not alter its membrane association (Figure 1c) – inhibits synchronized osteoclast fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The C-terminal half of La produced recombinantly and added to the medium bathing differentiating osteoclast precursors binds the surface of these cells.
source: Previously, we showed that the C-terminal half of La produced recombinantly and added to the medium bathing differentiating osteoclast precursors binds the surface of these cells and is sufficient to promote osteoclast fusion and resorptive function (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: The C-terminal half of La is sufficient to promote osteoclast fusion.
source: Previously, we showed that the C-terminal half of La produced recombinantly and added to the medium bathing differentiating osteoclast precursors binds the surface of these cells and is sufficient to promote osteoclast fusion and resorptive function (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: The C-terminal half of La is sufficient to promote resorptive function in osteoclasts.
source: Previously, we showed that the C-terminal half of La produced recombinantly and added to the medium bathing differentiating osteoclast precursors binds the surface of these cells and is sufficient to promote osteoclast fusion and resorptive function (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Reduction of recombinant La 194-408 greatly diminished its ability to promote osteoclast multinucleation.
source: When we compared the effects of La 194–408 vs reduced La 194–408 on primary human osteoclast multinucleation, we found that the reduction of recombinant La greatly diminished its ability to promote osteoclast multinucleation and resorption (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Reduction of recombinant La 194-408 greatly diminished its ability to promote osteoclast resorption.
source: When we compared the effects of La 194–408 vs reduced La 194–408 on primary human osteoclast multinucleation, we found that the reduction of recombinant La greatly diminished its ability to promote osteoclast multinucleation and resorption (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Human La has three cysteine residues.
source: Many of the effects of redox signaling are mediated by the oxidation of cysteine residues within proteins (van der Reest et al., 2018). Human La has three cysteine residues.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the protein sequence of human La.

claim: The N-terminal half of La (La 1–187), containing one of La's cysteines, is dispensable for La's role in promoting osteoclast fusion.
source: However, we have previously demonstrated that the N-terminal half of La (La 1–187), containing one of La's cysteines, is dispensable for La's role in promoting osteoclast fusion (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: A fraction of La 194–408 migrates as a band approximately twice the predicted size of La 194–408 despite separation via denaturing gel electrophoresis, suggesting the presence of La 194–408 dimers.
source: Interestingly, we find that a fraction of La 194–408 migrates as a band ~twice the predicted size of La 194–408 despite separation via denaturing gel electrophoresis, suggesting the presence of La 194–408 dimers (Berndt et al., 2021a; Craig et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an observation from gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with inference about dimers supported by citations.

claim: No dimer band is observed in La Cys Mut.
source: In contrast, we observe no dimer band in La Cys Mut (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is an observation from gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: The loss of Cys 232 and Cys 245 greatly diminishes the affinity of the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized La species.
source: In addition, we find that the loss of Cys 232 and Cys 245 greatly diminishes the affinity of the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized La species, whereas both species are recognized by an α-6xHis monoclonal antibody via their N-terminal His tags (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Both La 194-408 and La Cys Mut are recognized by an α-6xHis monoclonal antibody via their N-terminal His tags.
source: In addition, we find that the loss of Cys 232 and Cys 245 greatly diminishes the affinity of the α-La antibody that recognizes the oxidized La species, whereas both species are recognized by an α-6xHis monoclonal antibody via their N-terminal His tags (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The loss of Cys 232 and Cys 245 strongly abrogates the ability of La 194–408 to promote osteoclast fusion.
source: Finally, we found that the loss of Cys 232 and Cys 245 strongly abrogates the ability of La 194–408 to promote osteoclast fusion (Figure 4c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Cys 232 and Cys 245 are vital for La's function in osteoclast multinucleation.
source: From these data, we conclude that Cys 232 and Cys 245 – previously highlighted for their roles in redox-dependent structural changes in La (Berndt et al., 2021a) – are vital for La's function in osteoclast multinucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: The La pool within the nuclei of eukaryotic cells is primarily a reduced species.
source: The La pool within the nuclei of eukaryotic cells is primarily a reduced species (Berndt et al., 2021a; Berndt et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NAC treatment suppresses ROS elevation stimulated by RANKL-initiated differentiation of human osteoclasts.
source: We found that NAC treatment suppresses ROS elevation stimulated by RANKL-initiated differentiation of human osteoclasts (Figure 5a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: NAC treatment 24 hr after RANKL application did not lower the steady-state levels of osteoclastogenic differentiation factors (NFATc1 and cFOS).
source: While early treatment with NAC has been reported to disrupt the pre-fusion stages of osteoclast differentiation (Lee et al., 2005), we found that NAC treatment 24 hr after RANKL application (i.e., after early osteoclast precursor commitment), did not lower the steady-state levels of osteoclastogenic differentiation factors (NFATc1 and cFOS) or the transcripts of two fusion-related proteins (La or AnxA5) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: NAC treatment 24 hr after RANKL application did not lower the transcripts of two fusion-related proteins (La or AnxA5).
source: While early treatment with NAC has been reported to disrupt the pre-fusion stages of osteoclast differentiation (Lee et al., 2005), we found that NAC treatment 24 hr after RANKL application (i.e., after early osteoclast precursor commitment), did not lower the steady-state levels of osteoclastogenic differentiation factors (NFATc1 and cFOS) or the transcripts of two fusion-related proteins (La or AnxA5) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: NAC-mediated inhibition of ROS signaling suppresses osteoclast multinucleation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We then explored the effects of suppressing ROS signaling on osteoclast formation and the trafficking of La, as in Cao and Picklo, 2014; Kim et al., 2019, we found that NAC-mediated inhibition of ROS signaling suppresses osteoclast multinucleation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Suppressing ROS signaling with NAC inhibited the transition from reduced to oxidized, cytoplasmic La species.
source: Suppressing ROS signaling with NAC also inhibited the transition from reduced to oxidized, cytoplasmic La species, as evidenced by decrease in staining of permeabilized osteoclasts with α-oxidized La antibody and a complementary increase in staining of permeabilized osteoclasts with α-reduced La antibody (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-d.

claim: NAC application inhibited the cell surface delivery of La in human osteoclasts.
source: Most importantly, NAC application inhibited the cell surface delivery of La in human osteoclasts (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The transition from reduced to oxidized La species occurs inside the osteoclast cytoplasm during their commitment program rather than being a consequence of La arriving at the oxidizing environment of the extracellular milieu.
source: Moreover, our findings also indicate that the transition from reduced to oxidized La species occurs inside the osteoclast cytoplasm during their commitment program rather than being a consequence of La arriving at the oxidizing environment of the extracellular milieu.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing NAC inhibits cytoplasmic oxidized La and surface delivery.

claim: At the time of fusion, La is mostly dephosphorylated, as evidenced by a loss of the cell staining with antibodies specific for La phosphorylated at Ser366.
source: While most of La in human cells is phosphorylated at Ser 366 (Schwartz et al., 2004), at the time of fusion, La is mostly dephosphorylated, as evidenced by a loss of the cell staining with antibodies specific for La phosphorylated at Ser366 (α-p366 La Ab) (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: NAC suppression of transient ROS signaling greatly increases phosphorylated La in osteoclasts.
source: We find that while little phosphorylated La is typically observed in the nuclei of differentiating osteoclasts during fusion timepoints, that NAC suppression of transient ROS signaling greatly increases phosphorylated La in osteoclasts (Figure 6a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Inhibition of intracellular ROS generation prevents La dephosphorylation in differentiating osteoclast precursors.
source: These data indicate that inhibition of intracellular ROS generation prevents La dephosphorylation and the loss of nuclear localization in differentiating osteoclast precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Inhibition of intracellular ROS generation prevents the loss of nuclear localization of La in differentiating osteoclast precursors.
source: These data indicate that inhibition of intracellular ROS generation prevents La dephosphorylation and the loss of nuclear localization in differentiating osteoclast precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Application of La 194–408 to NAC-treated cells rescued osteoclast fusion inhibition.
source: Indeed, we found that application of La 194–408 to NAC-treated cells rescued osteoclast fusion inhibition (Figure 6c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: The ability of La 194–408 to rescue NAC-inhibited osteoclast fusion is at least partially dependent on Cys 232 and Cys 245.
source: However, the ability of La 194–408 to rescue NAC-inhibited osteoclast fusion is at l=east partially dependent on Cys 232 and Cys 245, as mutation of these residues to Ala greatly diminished the ability of La 194–408 to rescue NAC effects on fusion.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: ROS signaling plays a vital role in triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts.
source: Finding that the NAC-mediated ROS suppression of surface trafficking and fusion can be compensated for by the application of exogenous La strongly supports the conclusion that ROS signaling plays a vital role in triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts and the promotion of their multinucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments in Figure 6.

claim: ROS signaling plays a vital role in the promotion of osteoclast multinucleation.
source: Finding that the NAC-mediated ROS suppression of surface trafficking and fusion can be compensated for by the application of exogenous La strongly supports the conclusion that ROS signaling plays a vital role in triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts and the promotion of their multinucleation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Cys 232 and Cys 245 are vital for oxidized La's ability to promote osteoclast multinucleation and resorptive function.
source: Moreover, the loss of La's ability to rescue NAC suppression of osteoclast multinucleation when Cys 232 and Cys 245 are mutated to Ala also suggests that these residues are vital for oxidized La's ability to promote osteoclast multinucleation and resorptive function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: ROS signaling downstream of osteoclast commitment contributes to the cell fusion stage of osteoclast formation by promoting intracellular oxidation of La.
source: In summary, ROS signaling downstream of osteoclast commitment contributes to the cell fusion stage of osteoclast formation by promoting intracellular oxidation of La and its delivery to the surface of fusion-committed cells, where La promotes multinucleation and subsequent resorptive activity in human osteoclasts (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the Results section.

claim: ROS signaling downstream of osteoclast commitment contributes to the cell fusion stage of osteoclast formation by promoting delivery of La to the surface of fusion-committed cells.
source: In summary, ROS signaling downstream of osteoclast commitment contributes to the cell fusion stage of osteoclast formation by promoting intracellular oxidation of La and its delivery to the surface of fusion-committed cells, where La promotes multinucleation and subsequent resorptive activity in human osteoclasts (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the Results section.

claim: The reversible shift of redox homeostasis in cells to a moderately oxidized state regulates the function and localization of many proteins.
source: The reversible shift of redox homeostasis in cells to a moderately oxidized state, referred to as redox signaling, regulates the function and localization of many proteins and favors differentiation vs proliferation (Smith et al., 2000; Hansen and Harris, 2015; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Redox signaling favors differentiation vs proliferation.
source: The reversible shift of redox homeostasis in cells to a moderately oxidized state, referred to as redox signaling, regulates the function and localization of many proteins and favors differentiation vs proliferation (Smith et al., 2000; Hansen and Harris, 2015; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ROS signaling and its inhibition by NAC likely influence osteoclast formation in many ways and at many points in the formation of multinucleated osteoclasts.
source: ROS signaling and its inhibition by NAC likely influence osteoclast formation in many ways and at many points in the formation of multinucleated osteoclasts (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation based on established knowledge and citation.

claim: Exogenous La rescues the NAC-mediated suppression of osteoclast fusion.
source: However, our finding that exogenous La rescues the NAC-mediated suppression of osteoclast fusion supports the hypothesis that ROS signaling promotes cell fusion stage of osteoclastogenesis by triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: ROS signaling promotes cell fusion stage of osteoclastogenesis by triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts.
source: However, our finding that exogenous La rescues the NAC-mediated suppression of osteoclast fusion supports the hypothesis that ROS signaling promotes cell fusion stage of osteoclastogenesis by triggering La's delivery to the surface of osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The reduced species of La functions as an essential nuclear RNA chaperone.
source: While the reduced species of La functions as an essential nuclear RNA chaperone, oxidized La shifts to the cytoplasm and shuttles to the surface of the osteoclasts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about La protein function.

claim: Oxidized La shifts to the cytoplasm and shuttles to the surface of the osteoclasts.
source: While the reduced species of La functions as an essential nuclear RNA chaperone, oxidized La shifts to the cytoplasm and shuttles to the surface of the osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: The specialized oxidized species of cell surface-associated La promotes osteoclast fusion and bone resorption.
source: It is this specialized oxidize species of cell surface-associated La that promotes osteoclast fusion and bone resorption.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by oxidation-induced oligomerization of the protein.
source: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by many changes in the protein structure, including an oxidation-induced oligomerization of the protein, a loss of almost half of its helical content, and a change in accessibility of epitopes recognized by conformation specific antibodies (Berndt et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by a loss of almost half of its helical content.
source: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by many changes in the protein structure, including an oxidation-induced oligomerization of the protein, a loss of almost half of its helical content, and a change in accessibility of epitopes recognized by conformation specific antibodies (Berndt et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by a change in accessibility of epitopes recognized by conformation specific antibodies.
source: The transition from reduced to oxidized species of La is accompanied by many changes in the protein structure, including an oxidation-induced oligomerization of the protein, a loss of almost half of its helical content, and a change in accessibility of epitopes recognized by conformation specific antibodies (Berndt et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: La belongs to a category of fold switching proteins that change functions in response to the cellular environment.
source: Our data show that La belongs to a category of fold switching proteins that change functions in response to the cellular environment, more specifically, oxidizing and reducing intracellular conditions (Kim and Porter, 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study and supported by citation.

claim: Formation of multinucleated osteoclasts involves the caspase 3-cleaved, non-phosphorylated species of La.
source: In addition to direct changes in the structure of La caused by its oxidation, ROS can influence La function in osteoclast fusion by indirect effects. Formation of multinucleated osteoclasts involves the caspase 3-cleaved, non-phosphorylated species of La (Whitlock et al., 2023)
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: ROS can activate caspase 3.
source: ROS can influence La function in osteoclast fusion by indirect effects. Formation of multinucleated osteoclasts involves the caspase 3-cleaved, non-phosphorylated species of La (Whitlock et al., 2023) and ROS can influence La properties by activation of both caspase 3 (Liu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ROS can activate PP2A-like phosphatase.
source: ROS can influence La properties by activation of both caspase 3 (Liu et al., 2019) and PP2A-like phosphatase (Cicchillitti et al., 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PP2A-like phosphatase has been reported to dephosphorylate La Ser366 before La cleavage.
source: ROS can influence La properties by activation of both caspase 3 (Liu et al., 2019) and PP2A-like phosphatase (Cicchillitti et al., 2003), previously reported to dephosphorylate La Ser366 before La cleavage (Rutjes et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NAC inhibits dephosphorylation of La.
source: Indeed, while our finding that NAC inhibits dephosphorylation of La can indicate that redox-dependent changes in La's conformation are required for the dephosphorylation of the protein, it can also be explained by the ROS dependence of PP2A activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Redox-dependent changes in La's conformation may be required for the dephosphorylation of the protein.
source: Indeed, while our finding that NAC inhibits dephosphorylation of La can indicate that redox-dependent changes in La's conformation are required for the dephosphorylation of the protein, it can also be explained by the ROS dependence of PP2A activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: La association with the cell surface does not change after reducing oxidized La with TCEP.
source: Furthermore, our finding that La association with the cell surface does not change after reducing oxidized La with TCEP argues against the hypothesis that La oxidation is merely required for its association with the surface of osteoclasts.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Formation of disulfide bonds, re-localization of normally nuclear proteins to the cytoplasm, extracellular medium, and cell surface, and dramatic changes in function in response to transient increases in ROS concentrations have been well described for other nuclear chaperones, in particular, high mobility group Box 1 (HMGB1).
source: Formation of disulfide bonds; re-localization of normally nuclear proteins to the cytoplasm, extracellular medium, and cell surface; and dramatic changes in function in response to transient increases in ROS concentrations have been well described for other nuclear chaperones, in particular, high mobility group Box 1 (HMGB1) (Kwak et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Like La, HMGB1 has three cysteines.
source: Like La, HMGB1 has three cysteines and mild HMGB1 oxidation generates disulfide bonds that stabilize homodimers (Kwak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mild HMGB1 oxidation generates disulfide bonds that stabilize homodimers.
source: Like La, HMGB1 has three cysteines and mild HMGB1 oxidation generates disulfide bonds that stabilize homodimers (Kwak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Homodimerization by formation of disulfide bonds is a pre-requisite for the unconventional secretion of Fibroblast Growth Factor 1.
source: Homodimerization by formation of disulfide bonds is also a pre-requisite for the unconventional secretion of Fibroblast Growth Factor 1 (Prudovsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Like redox signaling, NO signaling promotes osteoclastogenesis.
source: Interestingly, like redox signaling (Domazetovic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2005), NO signaling promotes osteoclastogenesis (Nilforoushan et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NO signaling promotes the translocation of La protein to the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, like redox signaling (Domazetovic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2005), NO signaling promotes osteoclastogenesis (Nilforoushan et al., 2009) and the translocation of La protein to the cytoplasm (Berndt et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Redox signaling induces changes in the location and function of La.
source: In conclusion, in this study, we identified redox signaling as a molecular switch that redirects La protein away from the nucleus, where it protects precursor tRNAs from exonuclease digestion, and toward its separable function at the osteoclast surface, where La regulates the multinucleation and resorptive functions of these managers of the skeleton.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: Proteins involved in osteoclastogenesis represent potential therapeutic targets for treating bone loss diseases.
source: Proteins involved in osteoclastogenesis represent potential therapeutic targets for treating bone loss diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about therapeutic potential.

claim: Osteoclast La acts at a different location from the species of La that carries out its essential and ubiquitous RNA chaperoning functions (cell surface vs nucleus).
source: Finding that osteoclast La promotes bone resorption by acting not only at a different location but also in a different conformation from in comparison to the species of La that carries out its essential and ubiquitous RNA chaperoning functions (cell surface vs nucleus and oxidized vs reduced form), may help in minimizing off target effects of La targeting treatments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Osteoclast La acts in a different conformation from the species of La that carries out its essential and ubiquitous RNA chaperoning functions (oxidized vs reduced form).
source: Finding that osteoclast La promotes bone resorption by acting not only at a different location but also in a different conformation from in comparison to the species of La that carries out its essential and ubiquitous RNA chaperoning functions (cell surface vs nucleus and oxidized vs reduced form), may help in minimizing off target effects of La targeting treatments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: On average, small multinucleated syncytia appear 2 days after RANKL application in primary human monocyte cultures.
source: While the time course and efficiency of multinucleated osteoclast formation vary from donor to donor (Whitlock et al., 2023), on average, we observed the appearance of small, multinucleated syncytia 2 days after RANKL application and fusion rapidly increased over the next 2 days, resulting in mature, resorption competent osteoclasts at 4–5 days post-RANKL addition (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study and previous work.

claim: Fusion rapidly increases over 2 days following the appearance of small multinucleated syncytia, resulting in mature, resorption competent osteoclasts at 4–5 days post-RANKL addition.
source: While the time course and efficiency of multinucleated osteoclast formation vary from donor to donor (Whitlock et al., 2023), on average, we observed the appearance of small, multinucleated syncytia 2 days after RANKL application and fusion rapidly increased over the next 2 days, resulting in mature, resorption competent osteoclasts at 4–5 days post-RANKL addition (Whitlock et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study and previous work.

claim: The cell fusion stage of multinucleated osteoclast formation depends on La trafficking to the surface of the osteoclasts at days 2–4 post-RANKL application.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that the cell fusion stage of multinucleated osteoclast formation depends on La trafficking to the surface of the osteoclasts at days 2–4 post-RANKL application (Whitlock et al., 2023)
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.
